## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals today. You learn how to handle raw and tidy data in R, how to import
data into R using `data.table::fread()`, and how to save data again.

One note up front, and it connects to the AI session: importing data is an area
in which using AI tools becomes particularly helpful — but only once you
understand the basics of how importing works and what to keep an eye on.
Otherwise you cannot tell a correct import from a plausible-looking but wrong
one, and a wrong import silently poisons everything downstream.

## Slide 4 · The role of data preparation

Importing and preparing data is the most fundamental task in data science, and it
is also largely under-appreciated — it is what you spend most of your time on and
what nobody writes papers about.

Recall the cycle from the first session: data preparation and processing,
visualisation, and analysis and modelling feed into each other, and everything
funnels into the presentation of the insights as one overall story.

Today we deal with the very first step of that cycle: how to get the raw data
into R, and how to get the result back out into the file system.

## Slide 5 · Focus of this session

We use the directory structure introduced in the session on project management,
and we learn how to import data using the most widely used file formats,
especially csv.

The goal is the one you already know: all results must be reproducible from the
raw data at any time. This implies that you must not manipulate your raw data at
any cost. Raw data is what you download from the internet, gather through an
experiment, or code yourself.

This session sits between two others: it builds on the session on project
management, and it precedes the session on data preparation.

## Slide 6 · Recap: how to keep your work transparent

A quick recap from the project-management session, because everything today rests
on it.

Raw data must not be changed, but it is usually not in a state we can work with.
So: gather the data and save it, import it into R, write a script that transforms
the raw data into tidy data, and use the tidy data for the analysis.

Saving the scripts in steps two and three makes your work fully reproducible. By
looking into the script you will always know what you did to your raw data, which
means you can heal basically every mistake you made — no harm done. That is the
whole payoff of never touching the raw file.

## Slide 8 · Preparation: set up your working environment

Before importing anything, set up the working environment as we discussed.

Raw data should be saved in `data/raw`. If you have very few data sets you might
get away with a single `data` folder, but the split pays off quickly.

Tidied-up data should be saved in `data/tidy` — keep it strictly separate from
the raw data, so that you can always tell at a glance which files you may
overwrite and which you may not.

## Slide 9 · Import functions

The function we use to import a data set depends on the file type.

For csv and tsv files we use `data.table::fread()`. For R's own formats, Rds and
RData, there are `readRDS()` and `load()`. And for the formats of other
statistical packages — Stata, SAS, SPSS — the `haven` package provides
specialised functions, which is what you need when you get data from colleagues
in economics or the social sciences.

The basic procedure is the same in all cases, so we focus on reading csv files
here. In the following we assume that your raw data is stored in the folder
`data/raw`.

## Slide 10 · How to import data

Good practice is to save the path to the file in a vector first, using
`here::here()`, and then pass that vector to the import function. This keeps the
path in one place and makes the import call readable.

Since it is a csv file we use `data.table::fread()`. In general I recommend using
`fread()` — it is fast and it guesses well — but alternatives are available,
including from the tidyverse.

Written like this, the call uses default options to import the file. That works
often for clean data files. But for the sake of transparency, and because data
files are very often not clean, we should specify several optional arguments
explicitly. That is what the rest of this session is about.

## Slide 11 · Exercise 1

First exercise. Download the zip file from the course homepage, extract it inside
`data/raw/` in your R project, and write a script that imports
`fread_expls-1.csv` into your session.

Put the script into the folder `R`, and start it with `here::i_am()` as usual.
The first file is the clean one, so the default options should get you there.

## Slide 12 · The four arguments that matter

Four arguments carry almost all of the work, and we go through them one by one.

`file` is the relative path to the csv file you want to read — always via
`here::here()`. `sep` is the symbol that separates the columns. `dec` is the
symbol used as the decimal sign. And `colClasses` says what object type should be
used for each of the columns.

For other widely used arguments check the tutorial and do the exercises, and note
that there are even more specification options — `help(fread)` lists them all.

## Slide 13 · `sep`: the column separator

The first argument is `sep`, the column separator.

Especially in Germany, columns are often separated via a semicolon instead of a
comma — which is ironic, given that csv stands for comma-separated values. The
reason is the next slide's topic.

We can pass a string to `sep` indicating how the columns are separated. In the
case on the slide, `sep = ";"`.

If you get a data frame with exactly one column whose name is a long string
containing semicolons, this is what went wrong.

## Slide 14 · `dec`: the decimal sign

And here is the reason for the semicolons: in Germany, decimal places are often
separated via a comma instead of a point. If the decimal sign is already a comma,
the comma is no longer available as a column separator — hence the semicolon.

We pass a string to `dec` to say which symbol is used as the decimal sign.

The failure mode here is subtler than with `sep` and therefore more dangerous:
your numbers may be read as character, or — worse — silently truncated. Always
check the column types after importing.

## Slide 15 · Exercise 2

Second exercise. Import `fread_expls-2.csv` such that exactly this tibble
results.

Pay attention to the types in the second row of the output: `c_code` is
character, `year` is integer, and the two remaining columns are double. If your
`exports` column comes out as character, the decimal sign is the culprit.

## Slide 16 · `colClasses`: the column types

The third argument is `colClasses`, and this is the one that catches real data
most often.

Whenever numbers should be saved as character, the guessing algorithm of
`fread()` fails. Look at the product code on the left: `0011`. It is a code, not
a quantity — the leading zeros are part of its identity. But `fread()` sees
digits, decides the column is integer, and the code becomes the number eleven.
The leading zeros are gone and you cannot get them back.

We can specify the column types explicitly by passing a vector to `colClasses`,
one entry per column. Doing this is usually a good idea anyway, because it makes
your code more transparent: the reader sees what the data is supposed to look
like, and the import fails loudly if the file changes.

You can also combine it with `select` and read only selected columns — see the
tutorial.

## Slide 17 · Exercise 3

Third exercise, and this one is the realistic case: read in `fread_expls-3.csv`
using all the arguments you consider necessary, and make sure that the column
`cgroup` is stored as a factor.

The hint matters more than the exercise. Before importing an unknown file, look
at it in its raw form: click on the file in the Files pane and select "View
File". You then see the separators, the decimal signs and any header junk with
your own eyes, instead of guessing.

For very large files that is infeasible, so use `nrows` and `select` to read a
representative subset first, inspect that, and only then write the real import
call.

## Slide 19 · And what about saving data?

Saving data is much easier than reading data, because you already know
everything about the object you are saving — there is nothing to guess.

The only relevant question is the format. If there are no good arguments for
using a different format, go for csv: it is readable by every tool, it survives
software changes, and you can open it in a text editor in ten years.

This is achieved with `data.table::fwrite()`, which takes the object as `x` and
the file name as `file` — again via `here::here()`, and note that the result goes
into `data/tidy`, not into `data/raw`.

## Slide 20 · The general idea

To put the pieces together, and with a warning: make yourself comfortable before
reading in data, and expect frustration. Real files are messy, and getting them
in correctly takes longer than you think it should. That is normal and it is not
a sign that you are doing it wrong.

The general idea: you import the data and bind it to an R object — usually a
data.frame, or whatever aligns with your preferred dialect. Then you proceed with
transforming this object until it satisfies the demands for tidy data. Then you
save the data under a new name, save the script, and celebrate yourself.

Note "under a new name" once more: the raw file stays untouched.

We will cover the transformation steps in the next session.

## Slide 21 · Summary and conclusion

To summarise: you learned how to import data into R, with the main focus on
importing csv data files using `data.table::fread()`. Other functions for csv are
provided, for example via the tidyverse packages, and for other formats
specialised functions are available, especially in the haven package.

Importing standard data often works well with the default options. In other cases
the optional arguments must be used — and then you check the function
documentation rather than guessing.

If speed or memory restrictions are an issue, comparing import functions is
advisable; they differ considerably on large files.

And to close the loop with the opening note: once you understand the basics,
using AI to assist with coding becomes very useful in the context of data import.
You can describe the shape of the file and get a plausible `fread()` call back —
but you are the one who has to verify that the column types are right.
